claim: Plant cells are typically considered totipotent, in that a complete plant can be regenerated from nearly any isolated individual cell.
source: Plants exhibit remarkable developmental plasticity and their cells are typically considered totipotent, in that a complete plant can be regenerated from nearly any isolated individual cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plant cell biology.

claim: In intact plants, distinct cell lineages emerge and terminal fates are stable.
source: In intact plants, however, distinct cell lineages emerge and terminal fates are stable.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plant development.

claim: Asymmetric divisions of protodermal cells generate meristemoid mother cells (MMC) and meristemoids (M) in the Arabidopsis leaf epidermis.
source: A prime example of a specialized lineage is in the Arabidopsis leaf epidermis (Figure 1A) where asymmetric divisions of protodermal cells generate meristemoid mother cells (MMC) and meristemoids (M), self-renewing cells akin to transit amplifying cells in mammalian stem cell lineages (Lau and Bergmann, 2012; Pillitteri and Dong, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Meristemoids are self-renewing cells akin to transit amplifying cells in mammalian stem cell lineages.
source: A prime example of a specialized lineage is in the Arabidopsis leaf epidermis (Figure 1A) where asymmetric divisions of protodermal cells generate meristemoid mother cells (MMC) and meristemoids (M), self-renewing cells akin to transit amplifying cells in mammalian stem cell lineages (Lau and Bergmann, 2012; Pillitteri and Dong, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Meristemoids differentiate into guard mother cells (GMCs) at the end of their renewing stages.
source: At the end of their renewing stages, these meristemoids differentiate into guard mother cells (GMCs), which undergo a single symmetric division to generate the paired guard cells (GCs) of the mature stomata.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about stomatal development.

claim: Guard mother cells undergo a single symmetric division to generate the paired guard cells of the mature stomata.
source: At the end of their renewing stages, these meristemoids differentiate into guard mother cells (GMCs), which undergo a single symmetric division to generate the paired guard cells (GCs) of the mature stomata.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about stomatal development.

claim: Guard cells and each of the intermediate stages leading to their formation are characterized by distinct morphologies and unique gene expression profiles.
source: GCs and each of the intermediate stages leading to their formation are characterized by distinct morphologies and unique gene expression profiles, allowing experimental dissection of lineage progression in intact, developing organs (Lau and Bergmann, 2012; Pillitteri and Dong, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: FAMA is a master regulator of guard cell identity.
source: The basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor FAMA is a master regulator of guard cell identity; it is necessary and sufficient for GC fate acquisition and its epidermal expression is limited to GMCs and young GCs (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) and (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: FAMA is necessary and sufficient for guard cell fate acquisition.
source: The basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor FAMA is a master regulator of guard cell identity; it is necessary and sufficient for GC fate acquisition and its epidermal expression is limited to GMCs and young GCs (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) and (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FAMA epidermal expression is limited to GMCs and young GCs.
source: The basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) transcription factor FAMA is a master regulator of guard cell identity; it is necessary and sufficient for GC fate acquisition and its epidermal expression is limited to GMCs and young GCs (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) and (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In fama mutants, GMCs are made but fail to progress into GCs and instead continue dividing while maintaining expression of earlier fate markers.
source: GMCs are made in fama mutants, but they fail to progress into GCs and instead continue dividing while maintaining expression of earlier fate markers (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) and (Figure 1B, inset)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and shown in Figure 1B inset.

claim: Failure to make guard cells in fama mutants results in seedling lethality.
source: this failure to make GCs results in seedling lethality (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) and (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Overexpression of FAMA reprograms other cells into GC identity.
source: Overexpression of FAMA reprograms other cells into GC identity, while simultaneously repressing cell division to yield single-celled stomata (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Overexpression of FAMA represses cell division to yield single-celled stomata.
source: Overexpression of FAMA reprograms other cells into GC identity, while simultaneously repressing cell division to yield single-celled stomata (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FAMA's direct targets include cell cycle regulators and genes associated with mature guard cell function.
source: FAMA's direct targets include cell cycle regulators and genes associated with mature guard cell function (Hachez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FAMA has been shown to act as a transcriptional activator.
source: FAMA has been shown to act as a transcriptional activator (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) but can also participate in repression of certain cell cycle targets (Hachez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FAMA can participate in repression of certain cell cycle targets.
source: FAMA has been shown to act as a transcriptional activator (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) but can also participate in repression of certain cell cycle targets (Hachez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FAMA is required for the irreversible differentiation of guard cells.
source: Here we show that FAMA is required for the irreversible differentiation of GCs and that it fulfills this role through recruitment of the Arabidopsis Retinoblastoma homologue, RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED (RBR).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout.

claim: FAMA fulfills its role in irreversible differentiation of guard cells through recruitment of RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED (RBR).
source: Here we show that FAMA is required for the irreversible differentiation of GCs and that it fulfills this role through recruitment of the Arabidopsis Retinoblastoma homologue, RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED (RBR).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout.

claim: Point mutations that disrupt FAMA-RBR interactions render FAMA capable of promoting initial GC identity, but unable to maintain commitment.
source: Point mutations that disrupt FAMA-RBR interactions render FAMA capable of promoting initial GC identity, but unable to maintain commitment.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data with FAMALGK mutant.

claim: FAMA promotes binding of RBR to the regulatory regions of stomatal regulators whose genomic regions contain repressive chromatin marks.
source: By demonstrating FAMA-promoted binding of RBR to the regulatory regions of stomatal regulators whose genomic regions contain repressive chromatin marks, we define a molecular mechanism by which the ubiquitously expressed RBR is recruited to specific genomic contexts at specific times to regulate key developmental events.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by ChIP data.

claim: RBR is broadly expressed in Arabidopsis development.
source: RBR is broadly expressed in Arabidopsis development and reduction of RBR activity has been correlated with excess division and loss of cell identity in many different contexts, including the early stomatal lineage (Borghi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Reduction of RBR activity has been correlated with excess division and loss of cell identity in many different contexts, including the early stomatal lineage.
source: RBR is broadly expressed in Arabidopsis development and reduction of RBR activity has been correlated with excess division and loss of cell identity in many different contexts, including the early stomatal lineage (Borghi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In the epidermis of actively dividing young leaves, RBRp:RBR-CFP is expressed in all cell nuclei.
source: In the epidermis of actively dividing young leaves, RBRp:RBR-CFP (Cruz-Ramirez et al., 2012) is expressed in all cell nuclei; as the leaf matures, expression becomes restricted to stomatal lineage cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by citation and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: As the leaf matures, RBRp:RBR-CFP expression becomes restricted to stomatal lineage cells.
source: In the epidermis of actively dividing young leaves, RBRp:RBR-CFP (Cruz-Ramirez et al., 2012) is expressed in all cell nuclei; as the leaf matures, expression becomes restricted to stomatal lineage cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mosaic co-suppression of the RBRp:RBR-CFP transgene leads to loss of fluorescence and concomitant excessive divisions in the CFP-minus sectors.
source: Mosaic co-suppression of the RBRp:RBR-CFP transgene leads to loss of fluorescence and concomitant excessive divisions in the CFP-minus sectors, suggesting that RBR represses cell divisions in both the early lineage and the terminally differentiated GCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RBR represses cell divisions in both the early lineage and the terminally differentiated guard cells.
source: Mosaic co-suppression of the RBRp:RBR-CFP transgene leads to loss of fluorescence and concomitant excessive divisions in the CFP-minus sectors, suggesting that RBR represses cell divisions in both the early lineage and the terminally differentiated GCs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is inferred from the co-suppression data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: FAMAp:amiRNA-RBR guard cells underwent inappropriate extra divisions oriented transverse to the long axis of the cells.
source: To examine RBR's role specifically in the GCs, we drove expression of artificial microRNAs (amiRNAs) against RBR by the FAMA promoter. FAMAp:amiRNA-RBR GCs underwent inappropriate extra divisions oriented transverse to the long axis of the cells, while other epidermal cells were not affected, confirming a direct requirement for RBR in GCs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: FAMAp:amiRNA-RBR does not affect other epidermal cells.
source: FAMAp:amiRNA-RBR GCs underwent inappropriate extra divisions oriented transverse to the long axis of the cells, while other epidermal cells were not affected, confirming a direct requirement for RBR in GCs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a direct requirement for RBR in guard cells.
source: FAMAp:amiRNA-RBR GCs underwent inappropriate extra divisions oriented transverse to the long axis of the cells, while other epidermal cells were not affected, confirming a direct requirement for RBR in GCs (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and confirming phenotypes reported using different amiRNAs directed against RBR (Lee et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and by citation.

claim: FAMA encodes a canonical RBR binding motif (LxCxE).
source: FAMA encodes a canonical RBR binding motif (LxCxE) (Burkhart and Sage, 2008) that is conserved among dicot FAMA orthologs, but not in FAMA's closest paralogs SPEECHLESS (SPCH) and MUTE (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by citation and shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The LxCxE motif is conserved among dicot FAMA orthologs.
source: FAMA encodes a canonical RBR binding motif (LxCxE) (Burkhart and Sage, 2008) that is conserved among dicot FAMA orthologs, but not in FAMA's closest paralogs SPEECHLESS (SPCH) and MUTE (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The LxCxE motif is not conserved in FAMA's closest paralogs SPEECHLESS (SPCH) and MUTE.
source: FAMA encodes a canonical RBR binding motif (LxCxE) (Burkhart and Sage, 2008) that is conserved among dicot FAMA orthologs, but not in FAMA's closest paralogs SPEECHLESS (SPCH) and MUTE (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Wild-type FAMA can interact with RBR in BiFC assays.
source: In both assays, WT FAMA, but not a version bearing point mutations changing the Cysteine (C) and Glutamate (E) in the LxCxE motif to Glycine (G) and Lysine (K) (FAMALGK) could interact with RBR.
evidence: This is shown in BiFC assays in Figure 1G.

claim: FAMALGK cannot interact with RBR in BiFC assays.
source: In both assays, WT FAMA, but not a version bearing point mutations changing the Cysteine (C) and Glutamate (E) in the LxCxE motif to Glycine (G) and Lysine (K) (FAMALGK) could interact with RBR.
evidence: This is shown in BiFC assays in Figure 1G.

claim: Wild-type FAMA can interact with RBR in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: In both assays, WT FAMA, but not a version bearing point mutations changing the Cysteine (C) and Glutamate (E) in the LxCxE motif to Glycine (G) and Lysine (K) (FAMALGK) could interact with RBR.
evidence: This is shown in yeast two-hybrid assays in Figure 1H.

claim: FAMALGK cannot interact with RBR in yeast two-hybrid assays.
source: In both assays, WT FAMA, but not a version bearing point mutations changing the Cysteine (C) and Glutamate (E) in the LxCxE motif to Glycine (G) and Lysine (K) (FAMALGK) could interact with RBR.
evidence: This is shown in yeast two-hybrid assays in Figure 1H.

claim: FAMALGK can interact with its dimerization partner bHLH93.
source: Importantly, FAMALGK could still interact with its dimerization partner bHLH93 (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) (Figure 1G), indicating that the FAMALGK variant maintains its overall structural integrity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and supported by citation.

claim: The FAMALGK variant maintains its overall structural integrity.
source: Importantly, FAMALGK could still interact with its dimerization partner bHLH93 (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006) (Figure 1G), indicating that the FAMALGK variant maintains its overall structural integrity.
evidence: This is inferred from the ability of FAMALGK to interact with bHLH93.

claim: FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP is exclusively nuclear in young cotyledons and leaves.
source: In young cotyledons and leaves, FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP was exclusively nuclear.
evidence: This is observed in the study.

claim: FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP is first apparent in GMCs.
source: Like G/YFP-tagged versions of FAMA published previously (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006; Pillitteri et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2014a), FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP is first apparent in GMCs, remains highly expressed as the GMCs undergo cell division, and is downregulated as GCs mature such that stomata with clearly defined pores express the protein at low levels or not at all (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C and supported by citations.

claim: FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP remains highly expressed as the GMCs undergo cell division.
source: Like G/YFP-tagged versions of FAMA published previously (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006; Pillitteri et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2014a), FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP is first apparent in GMCs, remains highly expressed as the GMCs undergo cell division, and is downregulated as GCs mature such that stomata with clearly defined pores express the protein at low levels or not at all (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP is downregulated as GCs mature such that stomata with clearly defined pores express the protein at low levels or not at all.
source: Like G/YFP-tagged versions of FAMA published previously (Ohashi-Ito and Bergmann, 2006; Pillitteri et al., 2007; Lee et al., 2014a), FAMAp:FAMALGK-YFP is first apparent in GMCs, remains highly expressed as the GMCs undergo cell division, and is downregulated as GCs mature such that stomata with clearly defined pores express the protein at low levels or not at all (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: FAMALGK was sufficient to rescue fama lethality.
source: Plants of genotype fama;FAMApro:FAMALGK (hereafter referred to as FAMALGK plants) were recovered and were moderately healthy and fertile, though smaller than wild type, indicating that FAMALGK was sufficient to rescue fama lethality (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I.

claim: FAMALGK plants are moderately healthy and fertile, though smaller than wild type.
source: Plants of genotype fama;FAMApro:FAMALGK (hereafter referred to as FAMALGK plants) were recovered and were moderately healthy and fertile, though smaller than wild type, indicating that FAMALGK was sufficient to rescue fama lethality (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1I.

claim: In the GCs of rescued FAMALGK plants, excessive cell divisions, changes in cell morphology, and production of paired GCs inside of existing GCs were observed.
source: In the GCs of rescued FAMALGK plants, however, we observed excessive cell divisions, changes in cell morphology, and, most strikingly, production of paired GCs inside of existing GCs (Figure 1J–L and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, phenotypic classes 6–11).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1J–L and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The FAMALGK phenotype results from an orderly reiteration of stomatal lineage progression, not from chaotic or uncontrolled divisions and fate changes.
source: Notably, the FAMALGK phenotype results, not from chaotic or uncontrolled divisions and fate changes, but rather an orderly reiteration of stomatal lineage progression.
evidence: This is inferred from detailed analysis of markers and phenotypes.

claim: The FAMALGK phenotype manifests as a progressive increase in phenotypic severity with age.
source: This manifested itself as a progressive increase in phenotypic severity with age (Figure 1L) and by the appearance of stomatal lineage markers in patterns suggesting that the GCs reverted to MMC identity and proceeded through the intermediate stages of the pathway normally (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1L.

claim: In FAMALGK plants, GCs reverted to MMC identity and proceeded through the intermediate stages of the pathway normally.
source: This manifested itself as a progressive increase in phenotypic severity with age (Figure 1L) and by the appearance of stomatal lineage markers in patterns suggesting that the GCs reverted to MMC identity and proceeded through the intermediate stages of the pathway normally (Figure 2).
evidence: This is inferred from marker expression patterns shown in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of stomatal-promoting transcription factors (SPCH, MUTE, FAMA) in FAMALGK plants followed the normal temporal patterns.
source: Expression of stomatal-promoting transcription factors (SPCH, MUTE, FAMA, Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), stomatal-restricting signaling elements (TMM, EPF1, EPF2, Figure 3A–D), and general division reporters (CDKA1;1, Figure 2B–C) followed the normal temporal patterns, and ectopic GC divisions appeared to follow early lineage division rules.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of stomatal-restricting signaling elements (TMM, EPF1, EPF2) in FAMALGK plants followed the normal temporal patterns.
source: Expression of stomatal-promoting transcription factors (SPCH, MUTE, FAMA, Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), stomatal-restricting signaling elements (TMM, EPF1, EPF2, Figure 3A–D), and general division reporters (CDKA1;1, Figure 2B–C) followed the normal temporal patterns, and ectopic GC divisions appeared to follow early lineage division rules.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A–D.

claim: Expression of general division reporters (CDKA1;1) in FAMALGK plants followed the normal temporal patterns.
source: Expression of stomatal-promoting transcription factors (SPCH, MUTE, FAMA, Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), stomatal-restricting signaling elements (TMM, EPF1, EPF2, Figure 3A–D), and general division reporters (CDKA1;1, Figure 2B–C) followed the normal temporal patterns, and ectopic GC divisions appeared to follow early lineage division rules.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: Ectopic GC divisions in FAMALGK plants appeared to follow early lineage division rules.
source: Expression of stomatal-promoting transcription factors (SPCH, MUTE, FAMA, Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), stomatal-restricting signaling elements (TMM, EPF1, EPF2, Figure 3A–D), and general division reporters (CDKA1;1, Figure 2B–C) followed the normal temporal patterns, and ectopic GC divisions appeared to follow early lineage division rules.
evidence: This is inferred from marker expression and division patterns.

claim: When a 'reprogrammed' GC in FAMALGK plants produced two stomata, they were separated by a non-stomatal cell, indicating that spacing divisions occurred.
source: For example, when a 'reprogrammed' GC produced two stomata, they were separated by a non-stomatal cell, indicating that spacing divisions occurred.
evidence: This is observed in the study and indicates normal spacing division behavior.

claim: Distinct cell orientations characteristic of amplifying divisions were visible in FAMALGK plants.
source: Distinct cell orientations characteristic of amplifying divisions were also visible (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Polarized localization of BASL in the larger daughter of a GC division provides evidence for normal asymmetric divisions in FAMALGK plants.
source: Further evidence for normal asymmetric divisions is polarized localization of BASL (Dong et al., 2009) in the larger daughter of a GC division (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3E and supported by citation.

claim: Lobed GCs in FAMALGK plants are cells that are transdifferentiating into an epidermal pavement cell identity.
source: Based on the lack of expression of stomatal lineage markers (Figure 2D), we interpret the lobed GCs we observe at low, but significant, frequencies in FAMALGK plants (Figure 1K, inset, and Figure 1L) as cells that are transdifferentiating into an epidermal pavement cell identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of stomatal marker expression shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In FAMAp:amiRBR lines, excessive GC division was accompanied by elevation of cell cycle gene expression throughout the GCs.
source: In FAMAp:amiRBR lines, by contrast, excessive GC division was accompanied by elevation of cell cycle gene expression throughout the GCs (CDKA1;1, Figure 1E , CDKB1;1 and CDC6, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but only rarely by misexpression of early stomatal lineage markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In FAMAp:amiRBR lines, excessive GC division was only rarely accompanied by misexpression of early stomatal lineage markers.
source: In FAMAp:amiRBR lines, by contrast, excessive GC division was accompanied by elevation of cell cycle gene expression throughout the GCs (CDKA1;1, Figure 1E , CDKB1;1 and CDC6, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), but only rarely by misexpression of early stomatal lineage markers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Spacing and amplifying divisions were not seen in FAMAp:amiRBR cotyledon GCs at any appreciable frequency (<1/1000 GCs) in 6–12 day old plants.
source: Consistent with gene expression behaviors, spacing and amplifying divisions were not seen in FAMAp:amiRBR cotyledon GCs at any appreciable frequency (<1/1000 GCs) in 6–12 day old plants.
evidence: This is observed in the study.

claim: Expression of an additional copy of tagged RBR (RBR-CFP) does not alter divisions in the stomatal lineage.
source: Expression of an additional copy of tagged RBR (RBR-CFP), however, does not alter divisions in the stomatal lineage; we observed neither arrested cells nor hyperproliferating cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A–B.

claim: In FAMALGK plants, GCs that undergo extra divisions re-express RBR as would be expected from RBR's normal expression pattern in the early stomatal lineage.
source: In FAMALGK plants, GCs that undergo extra divisions re-express RBR as would be expected from RBR's normal expression pattern in the early stomatal lineage (Figure 4C–G).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C–G.

claim: There was a dramatic increase in expression levels for the stomatal precursor genes in FAMALGK plants.
source: There was a dramatic increase in expression levels for the stomatal precursor genes, but variable change in expression of mature GC genes, consistent with a situation in which the overproduction of GCs through repeated re-entry is balanced by the loss of identity of older GCs (Figure 5A, mature GC genes).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was variable change in expression of mature GC genes in FAMALGK plants, consistent with a situation in which the overproduction of GCs through repeated re-entry is balanced by the loss of identity of older GCs.
source: There was a dramatic increase in expression levels for the stomatal precursor genes, but variable change in expression of mature GC genes, consistent with a situation in which the overproduction of GCs through repeated re-entry is balanced by the loss of identity of older GCs (Figure 5A, mature GC genes).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and inferred from the data.

claim: FAMALGK was still capable of up-regulating several, but not all, of the direct targets reported in Hachez et al., 2011.
source: FAMALGK was also still capable of up-regulating several, but not all, of the direct targets reported in (Hachez et al., 2011) (Figure 5A, FAMA direct targets).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and supported by citation.

claim: There was no evidence that cells in FAMALGK plants were being reprogrammed into embryonic or other stem-cell-like fates.
source: When expression of shoot meristem (SHOOT MERISTEMLESS, STM), root meristem (WUS HOMEOBOX, WOX5) or embryo genes (WOX9, WOX2, FUSCA3 (FUS3), LEC1) (Breuninger et al., 2008; De Smet et al., 2010) was monitored in FAMALGK plants, however, we found no evidence that cells were being reprogrammed into embryonic or other stem-cell-like fates (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: Disruption of FAMA-RBR interaction via the FAMALGK modification leads to a stomatal lineage-specific loss of terminal commitment.
source: Taken together, the gene expression data indicate that disruption of FAMA-RBR interaction via the FAMALGK modification leads to a stomatal lineage-specific loss of terminal commitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the gene expression data.

claim: H3K27me3 (a chromatin mark associated with transcriptional repression) is present in the genomic regions of SPCH, MUTE, FAMA, EPF1 and other stomatal genes in maturing leaves.
source: Analysis of chromatin states in maturing leaves revealed H3K27me3 (a chromatin mark associated with transcriptional repression) in the genomic regions of SPCH, MUTE, FAMA, EPF1 and other stomatal genes (Lafos et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Manipulation of a member of the POLYCOMB REPRESSIVE COMPLEX 2 (PRC2) can alter developmental regulation of H3K27me3 deposition at SPCH and MUTE loci.
source: a recent report showed that manipulation of a member of the POLYCOMB REPRESSIVE COMPLEX 2 (PRC2) can alter developmental regulation of H3K27me3 deposition at SPCH and MUTE loci (Lee et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Animal and plant Rb/RBR proteins can serve as interaction bridges between chromatin modifying enzymes and specific genomic contexts.
source: Animal and plant Rb/RBR proteins can serve as interaction bridges between chromatin modifying enzymes and specific genomic contexts (Burkhart and Sage, 2008; Gutzat et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RBR was previously found to be associated with SPCH regulatory regions via ChIP in whole seedlings.
source: RBR was previously found to be associated with SPCH regulatory regions via ChIP in whole seedlings (Weimer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FAMA (with RBR) ensures terminal differentiation of GCs by facilitating stable repression of early stomatal lineage genes.
source: Therefore it is plausible that, as the final master regulator bHLH in the stomatal pathway, FAMA (with RBR) ensures terminal differentiation of GCs by facilitating stable repression of early stomatal lineage genes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data and previous knowledge.

claim: SPCH, FAMA and EPF1 were all targets of FAMA in ChIP assays.
source: In ChIP assays, SPCH, FAMA and EPF1 were all targets of FAMA and of stomatal lineage-expressed RBR (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: SPCH, FAMA and EPF1 were all targets of stomatal lineage-expressed RBR in ChIP assays.
source: In ChIP assays, SPCH, FAMA and EPF1 were all targets of FAMA and of stomatal lineage-expressed RBR (Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: FAMA and RBR are enriched in the same pattern at SPCH and EPF1, suggesting that they bind as part of the same complex.
source: Further dissection of the binding regions at SPCH and EPF1 indicates that FAMA and RBR are enriched in the same pattern, suggesting that they bind as part of the same complex (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4 and inferred from the data.

claim: RBR enrichment at the promoters of SPCH and FAMA was significantly reduced in a FAMALGK background.
source: ChIPs of FAMAp:RBR-MYC in a FAMALGK background showed that RBR enrichment at the promoters of SPCH and FAMA, but not of the general RBR target gene PCNA, was significantly reduced (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4), consistent with our recruitment model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: RBR enrichment at the promoter of PCNA was not reduced in a FAMALGK background.
source: ChIPs of FAMAp:RBR-MYC in a FAMALGK background showed that RBR enrichment at the promoters of SPCH and FAMA, but not of the general RBR target gene PCNA, was significantly reduced (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4), consistent with our recruitment model.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: RBR enrichment at the promoter of EPF1 was variable in FAMALGK background assays.
source: RBR enrichment at the promoter of a negative regulator of stomatal development, EPF1, was more variable in our assays, sometimes showing little change (Figure 5D), but failing to associate with RBR in other replicates (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: SPCH is required for initiation of the stomatal lineage in normal development.
source: The association of FAMA and RBR with the SPCH locus is intriguing, as in normal development SPCH is required for initiation of the stomatal lineage and is essential for robust expression of all stomatal genes so far reported (MacAlister et al., 2007; Pillitteri et al., 2007; Kanaoka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SPCH is essential for robust expression of all stomatal genes so far reported.
source: The association of FAMA and RBR with the SPCH locus is intriguing, as in normal development SPCH is required for initiation of the stomatal lineage and is essential for robust expression of all stomatal genes so far reported (MacAlister et al., 2007; Pillitteri et al., 2007; Kanaoka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Expression of FAMAp:SPCH-YFP (or its hyperactive variants FAMAp:SPCH1-4A or FAMAp:SPCH2-4A) in an otherwise WT background did not mimic FAMALGK.
source: Expression of FAMAp:SPCH-YFP (or its hyperactive variants FAMAp:SPCH1-4A or FAMAp:SPCH2-4A [Lampard et al., 2008]) in an otherwise WT background, however, did not mimic FAMALGK (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E and supported by citation.

claim: Competence to reinitiate the stomatal pathway requires more than expression of a single 'trigger' gene, but rather a more generally permissive expression state.
source: This suggests that competence to reinitiate the stomatal pathway requires more than expression of a single 'trigger' gene, but rather a more generally permissive expression state, a fact supporting a broader chromatin regulating role for the FAMA-RBR complex (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and illustrated in Figure 5F.

claim: Physical associations between RBR and the Arabidopsis transcription factor SCARECROW (SCR) were found to be essential for modulating stem-cell behavior in the root.
source: Recently, physical associations between RBR and the Arabidopsis transcription factor SCARECROW (SCR) were found to be essential for modulating stem-cell behavior in the root (Cruz-Ramirez et al., 2012, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Both SCR and FAMA bind to RBR via an LxCxE motif.
source: Both SCR and FAMA bind to RBR via an LxCxE motif, yet the consequences of these transcription factor/RBR interactions are different
evidence: This is stated based on the study's findings and previous work.

claim: RBR antagonizes SCR function in asymmetric division in the root stem cell compartment.
source: RBR antagonizes SCR function in asymmetric division in the root stem cell compartment (Cruz-Ramirez et al., 2012, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: RBR and FAMA have similar functions promoting differentiation at the terminal stage of stomatal development.
source: whereas RBR and FAMA have similar functions promoting differentiation at the terminal stage of stomatal development.
evidence: This is a finding of the study.

claim: RBR is required for repression of SCR target genes.
source: As with FAMA targets, RBR is required for repression of SCR target genes and can associate with their promoter regions
evidence: This is stated based on previous work.

claim: RBR can associate with the promoter regions of SCR target genes.
source: As with FAMA targets, RBR is required for repression of SCR target genes and can associate with their promoter regions
evidence: This is stated based on previous work.

claim: RBR is associated with the promoter of the stomatal lineage initiator SPCH in cells as they are committing to terminal fates.
source: In this study, we provide key data in support of a specific molecular mechanism for transcriptional repression utilizing RBR in combination with cell-type specific transcription factors: first, we demonstrate, through cell-type specific ChIPs, that RBR is associated with the promoter of the stomatal lineage initiator SPCH in cells as they are committing to terminal fates
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through ChIP experiments.

claim: RBR binding to SPCH promoter is reduced when RBR's interaction with FAMA is disrupted.
source: and second, we show that this binding is reduced when RBR's interaction with FAMA is disrupted.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study demonstrated through ChIP experiments.

claim: RBR is recruited by cell-type specific transcription factors to lead to transcriptional repression of their targets.
source: Thus, our data provide strong support for RBR being recruited by cell-type specific transcription factors to lead to transcriptional repression of their targets (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data and illustrated in Figure 5F.

claim: There may be FAMA-independent ways to recruit RBR to the EPF1 locus.
source: This could indicate that there are FAMA-independent ways to recruit RBR to this site, or that our FAMALGK manipulation does not eliminate all FAMA-RBR interactions in the endogenous complex.
evidence: This is speculation based on the variable results for EPF1.

claim: The FAMALGK manipulation may not eliminate all FAMA-RBR interactions in the endogenous complex.
source: This could indicate that there are FAMA-independent ways to recruit RBR to this site, or that our FAMALGK manipulation does not eliminate all FAMA-RBR interactions in the endogenous complex.
evidence: This is speculation based on the variable results for EPF1.

claim: EPF1 is a repressor of stomatal development.
source: It is interesting, however, that EPF1 differs from SPCH and FAMA in being a repressor of stomatal development and thus alleviation of the repression of EPF1 would be expected to antagonize reprogramming to a stomatal precursor identity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Alleviation of the repression of EPF1 would be expected to antagonize reprogramming to a stomatal precursor identity.
source: It is interesting, however, that EPF1 differs from SPCH and FAMA in being a repressor of stomatal development and thus alleviation of the repression of EPF1 would be expected to antagonize reprogramming to a stomatal precursor identity.
evidence: This is inferred from the known function of EPF1.

claim: The role of PRC2 complex protein CURLY LEAF (CLF) was recently investigated in connection to stomatal lineage termination.
source: The role of PRC2 complex protein CURLY LEAF (CLF) was recently investigated in connection to stomatal lineage termination and was found to promote the accumulation of H3K27me3 marks on early stomatal lineage genes (Lee et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: CURLY LEAF (CLF) promotes the accumulation of H3K27me3 marks on early stomatal lineage genes.
source: The role of PRC2 complex protein CURLY LEAF (CLF) was recently investigated in connection to stomatal lineage termination and was found to promote the accumulation of H3K27me3 marks on early stomatal lineage genes (Lee et al., 2014b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Prolonged expression of a C-terminal GFP-tagged version of FAMA (FAMAtrans) causes phenotypes similar to, but milder than those seen in FAMALGK.
source: Additionally, (Lee et al., 2014b) report phenotypes, similar to, but milder than those seen in FAMALGK, caused by prolonged expression of a C-terminal GFP-tagged version of FAMA (FAMAtrans).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In 12 day old cotyledons, FAMALGK plants display reprogramming of ∼80% guard cells compared with 10% of FAMAtrans.
source: In a timepoint and tissue common to their data and this study (12 day old cotyledons), FAMALGK plants display reprogramming of ∼80% guard cells (Figure 1L) compared with 10% of FAMAtrans.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1L and compared to data from Lee et al., 2014b.

claim: Blocking of the FAMA C-terminus by addition of GFP creates a protein that dominantly interferes with FAMA-RBR interactions.
source: In light of our data showing that a loss of a specific FAMA activity (RBR binding) produces strong lineage reprogramming, we think a more parsimonious explanation of the FAMAtrans-induced phenotype is that blocking of the FAMA C-terminus by addition of GFP creates a protein that dominantly interferes with FAMA-RBR interactions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FAMAtrans phenotype based on the study's findings.

claim: Depletion of RBR in many contexts leads to hyperproliferation and derepression of cell cycle promoting genes.
source: Notably, depletion of RBR in many contexts leads to hyperproliferation and derepression of cell cycle promoting genes (Figure 1E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Borghi et al., 2010; Wachsman et al., 2011; Weimer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: When RBR's association with FAMA is disrupted, specific cell fates and division behaviors and their accompanying gene expression patterns re-emerge in an orderly pattern.
source: This is in contrast to phenotypes that dominate when its association with FAMA is disrupted; namely that specific cell fates and division behaviors and their accompanying gene expression patterns re-emerge in an orderly pattern.
evidence: This is a finding of the study.

claim: RBRp:RBR-CFP becomes ectopically expressed in re-dividing FAMALGK GCs.
source: RBRp:RBR-CFP itself becomes ectopically expressed in re-dividing FAMALGK GCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C–G.

claim: RBR's cell-cycle repressive role in FAMALGK GCs would be expected to completely halt divisions if it were playing that role.
source: Were RBR to be playing its cell-cycle repressive role in this context, one would expect this ectopic expression might completely halt divisions.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on RBR's known function.

claim: RBR plays a qualitatively different role in combination with FAMA in guard cells than its typical cell-cycle repressive role.
source: That the opposite occurs, however, suggests a qualitatively different role for RBR in combination with FAMA in these cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that divisions continue despite RBR expression.

claim: RBR's cell-cycle repression activity is more sensitive to dosage than its activity modulating stomatal gene expression.
source: Because RBR is expressed in all cells of the plant, it is difficult to measure whether our cell-type specific amiRNA completely eliminated RBR in guard cells, but our data suggest that RBR's cell-cycle repression activity is more sensitive to dosage than its activity modulating stomatal gene expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of RBR manipulation.

claim: Only by retaining RBR levels but disrupting the FAMA-dependent activity was a clear role for RBR in terminal differentiation unmasked.
source: Only by retaining RBR levels but disrupting the FAMA-dependent activity was a clear role for RBR in terminal differentiation unmasked.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's experimental design and results.

claim: Regulation of the stomatal lineage can parallel that of stem cell populations in animals at cellular, developmental and molecular levels.
source: Regulation of the stomatal lineage can parallel that of stem cell populations in animals at cellular, developmental and molecular levels.
evidence: This is stated as a general observation.

claim: Both plant stomatal and mammalian myogenic lineages employ series of paralogous bHLHs during fate specification and differentiation.
source: Both plant stomatal and mammalian myogenic lineages, for example, employ series of paralogous bHLHs during fate specification and differentiation, and activities of these bHLHs are regulated through conserved upstream kinases and by association with Rb/RBR (reviewed in Matos and Bergmann, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Activities of bHLHs in stomatal and myogenic lineages are regulated through conserved upstream kinases and by association with Rb/RBR.
source: Both plant stomatal and mammalian myogenic lineages, for example, employ series of paralogous bHLHs during fate specification and differentiation, and activities of these bHLHs are regulated through conserved upstream kinases and by association with Rb/RBR (reviewed in Matos and Bergmann, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review.

claim: Stomatal lineage cells leave a record of their fate and division history in their marker expression and spatial arrangement on the leaf surface.
source: Bound by immobile cell walls, stomatal lineage cells leave a record of their fate and division history in their marker expression and spatial arrangement on the leaf surface.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the stomatal lineage system.

claim: The stomatal lineage provides a unique opportunity to dissect cell division and cell fate activities of Rb and other conserved proteins during programming and reprogramming.
source: This plant model, therefore, provides a unique opportunity to dissect cell division and cell fate activities of Rb and other conserved proteins during programming and reprogramming and is a powerful comparative system for future discoveries of fundamental regulatory mechanisms of stem cell initiation, maintenance and termination.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the stomatal lineage as a model system.
